newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria sold 30 small state firms in 18 months.
newsitem.headline: Algeria sold 30 small state firms in 18 months.

text.p: Algeria, whose slow progress in privatisation has come under fire, sold 30 small, state-owned businesses and shed shares in 88 other companies in the past 18 months, the country's prime minister said on Wednesday.

Ahmed Ouyahia, who was quoted by the official Algerian news agency APS as addressing the government-appointed Transitional National Council (CNT), a quasi-parliament, gave no details on the sales but said privatisation still faced hurdles.
"Privatisation necessitates enterprise, adaptability to the new trend, and also needs more financial means and reasonable measures," Ouyahia said without elaborating.

Privatisation, adopted as a major policy some 18 months ago, is a thorny economic issue in Algeria. The authorities fear a mass sell-off might bring more upheaval to the delicate balance of civil strife locking the government in conflict with Moslem guerrillas.
The government worries that a speeded-up privatisation of state-owned companies which dominate the economy might lead to mass redundances, fuelling popular discontent.

The country has been gripped by violence for the past five years during which about 60,000 people have died. Officials have said that poverty and lack of jobs and houses drove many young people into the ranks of armed Moslem fundamentalists trying to turn the North African country into a strict Moslem state.

President Liamine Zeroual late in 1996 expressed dismay at the slow pace of privatisation. But his government rejected World Bank experts' recipe for mass privatisation of around 1,350 enterprises seen as saleable through "privatisation vouchers".

The man in charge of privatisation, Abderrahmane Mebtoul, who defends a "case by case" approach in shedding state-owned business, told the Algerian newspaper Le Soir d'Algerie on Tuesday the privatisation law needed to be changed as it limited the process.
Algeria has complex privatisation rules allowing for share transfers, management buyouts and complete sale of some enterprises to outside investors.
The state-owned enterprises sold so far range from a meduim-sized hotel and local authorities-controlled firms to state-run Entreprises des Galeries, a chain of supermarket-type stores.
